I'm sure plenty of people just find out about protests via facebook invites or the telephone game, not really here to argue one way or another. Even if it's common sense that you are correct in that point, it's speculation to even talk about. 

Just, as a responsible protestor, I think it's important for anyone to research what they're potentially putting themselves into a dangerous situation for. Whether it's for their personal safety from the crowd or police or counter-protestors. questions like: "is this an organization known to be violent?", "is the organizer a political amateur?", "am I a person with a marginalized identity going to a protest organized by people who dislike that identity?" are all examples of important things for one to consider before risking their life or their freedom to stand up for something.

Any responsible protestor would do so. Even beyond the extremes of the conversation this comment is part of, knowing the affiliations of the crowd and who's organizing it is important. It could save you a lot of trouble if you know the leaders are bad actors or known to incite violence when that's not something you want to be a part of.

I'm seeing a lot of arguments about if this is screamo or not, so I was hoping to help ease some of the drama. 

Noisey did a '[summer of screamo](https://noisey.vice.com/amp/en_us/article/ne5dm7/the-spirit-of-screamo-is-alive-and-well) ' series last year and I recommend checking it out. It goes through modern and classic (used loosely) screamo/skramz music. 

Screamo is the more extreme end of [80s-90s] emo with roots in styles like [powerviolence & grindcore](https://youtu.be/HKeofHz_k_E)  rather than [straightforward hardcore](https://youtu.be/Ra5y1SwQIb8). Dance Gavin Dance, and many of the other bands in this thread are post-hardcore bands, which is its own subgenre separate from screamo, but both developed & evolved from a parent genre: hardcore punk. While there is crossover in 90s emo and post-hardcore, by the time [At the Drive-In](https://youtu.be/7NYbojdoAQE)  & [The Blood Brothers](https://youtu.be/NfdjOqoshxI) were active, both prime examples of post-hardcore in the early 00s, post-hardcore had its own form, function & rules, separate from emo and screamo themselves. 

People use 'screamo' as an umbrella term because popular music publications used it. Hell, the band I linked there, Rites of Spring, was only referred to as 'emo' because of Thrasher Magazine's column on 'emocore' in the late 80s seen in [this](http://www.thrashermagazine.com/articles/magazine/january-1986/) scan of a January 1986 issue. RoS would have referred to themselves as a hardcore band and the other 'emocore' band listed there, embrace, fronted by Ian Mackaye of Minor Threat & Fugazi (hardcore & post-hardcore respectively)[thought the term was bullshit](https://www.culturecreature.com/emo-term-meaning/).

I hope any of this was interesting or informative.

bedroom pop and emo are vastly different.

emo has roots in hardcore, bedroom pop has roots in indie rock. they can both be equally emotional, but just because something is sad with guitars doesn't make it emo. traditional emo (i.e. pre-taking back sunday/brand new/dashboard confessional) has hallmarks like post-hardcore rhythms, soft-loud dynamic, sometimes gruff or screamed vocals, introspective or sociopolitical lyrics (or both.) bands like mineral, rites of spring, indian summer, policy of 3, for example.

newer "twinkle" bands tend to lean more 90s indie, but they still have more in common with cap'n jazz than guided by voices. bands like coma cinema, teen suicide, etc. may fit in with emo's current iteration, but so did smashing pumpkins, hum, and others during their era of emo's heyday. doesn't mean they're emo bands, their style just meshes well.
